92.explanation: In ITIL, the user is the consumer role that directly uses the service day-to-day for their activities. Distinct from the customer (defines requirements) and sponsor (funds).

A.text: The sponsor
A.rationale: The sponsor authorises funding; they do not necessarily use the service.

B.text: The user
B.rationale: Exact wording - user = direct daily usage.

C.text: The provider
C.rationale: The provider delivers; not in the user role.

D.text: The product owner
D.rationale: Product owner is on the provider side (product management), not the consumer side.

93.scenario: A service delivers every expected feature but becomes unavailable several hours each week.
93.question_text: Which aspect of the service is mainly insufficient?
93.explanation: ITIL distinguishes utility ("fit for purpose" - it does what you want) and warranty ("fit for use" - availability, capacity, security, continuity). A service that does the job but regularly goes down has OK utility but insufficient warranty.

A.text: Utility
A.rationale: Utility is OK - the expected features are there.

B.text: Warranty
B.rationale: Exact wording - warranty (availability) is deficient.

C.text: Value co-creation
C.rationale: Co-creation is a cross-cutting principle, not an aspect to evaluate here.

D.text: Value stream
D.rationale: A value stream describes a flow; it is not a "utility/warranty" aspect.

94.scenario: A new feature finally lets teams perform a task that was previously impossible.
94.explanation: Utility is "fit for purpose": what the service does, the functionality it enables. A new feature that makes a previously impossible task possible = utility by definition.

A.text: Warranty
A.rationale: Warranty = availability / security / continuity, not the function that becomes possible.

B.text: Utility
B.rationale: Exact wording - new capability = utility.

C.text: Governance
C.rationale: Governance = strategic steering, outside the utility/warranty pair.

D.text: Availability
D.rationale: Availability = warranty, not utility.

95.scenario: A user wants access to an application recently approved for their team.
95.question_text: Which element should mainly determine how this request is handled?
95.explanation: Service Requests are handled through predefined procedures documented in the catalogue and orchestration workflow - the very essence of Service Request Management (standardisation, predictability).

A.text: The organisation's predefined procedures
A.rationale: Exact wording - predefined procedures drive the handling.

B.text: The seniority of the requester
B.rationale: Absurd - seniority is not a standard criterion.

C.text: The cost of IT hardware
C.rationale: Off-topic - hardware cost does not steer the handling.

D.text: The network supplier
D.rationale: The network supplier has no direct influence on the workflow of an access request.

96.scenario: Two changes are planned simultaneously on the same critical infrastructure.
96.question_text: Which risk must be assessed as a priority?
96.explanation: Two changes planned at the same time on the same critical infrastructure = risk #1 = conflict (unexpected side effects, unplanned downtime). Change Enablement must detect this conflict and arbitrate.

A.text: The potential conflict between the changes
A.rationale: Exact wording - conflict = priority risk to assess.

B.text: The number of available technicians
B.rationale: Number of technicians = secondary risk, not a priority.

C.text: The number of registered users
C.rationale: Number of users = potential impact measure, not a conflict.

D.text: The duration of supplier contracts
D.rationale: Contract duration = not the immediate topic.

97.question_text: What is the main objective of relationship management?
97.explanation: Official objective of Relationship Management: establish and maintain links with stakeholders (customers, users, sponsors, communities) to understand their needs and expectations continuously.

A.text: Establish and maintain an understanding of stakeholder needs
A.rationale: Exact wording of the official objective.

B.text: Approve every change
B.rationale: Change approval = Change Authority (Change Enablement).

C.text: Resolve every incident
C.rationale: Resolving incidents = Incident Management.

D.text: Create service level agreements
D.rationale: Creating SLAs = Service Level Management.

98.scenario: An organisation depends heavily on a single provider for a critical service.
98.question_text: Which concern is the most relevant?
98.explanation: Heavy dependency on a single supplier for a critical service = concentration risk (vendor lock-in). Supplier Management must assess this risk and plan mitigations: strengthened contract, alternative, planned exit.

A.text: The risk of dependency on the supplier
A.rationale: Exact wording - dependency risk = concern #1.

B.text: The number of user tickets
B.rationale: Number of tickets = activity measure, not strategic risk.

C.text: The structure of the HR teams
C.rationale: HR structure = not the immediate topic.

D.text: The service catalogue
D.rationale: Catalogue = visibility of the offering, not supplier risk management.

99.question_text: Which characteristic best describes a successful improvement according to ITIL?
99.explanation: ITIL: a successful improvement delivers measurable value to stakeholders. It is the single success criterion - not the means (automation), not secondary objectives (cost).

A.text: It delivers measurable value to stakeholders
A.rationale: Exact wording - measurable value = ITIL success criterion.

B.text: It automates every activity
B.rationale: Automation is a means, not the measure of success.

C.text: It always reduces costs
C.rationale: False - some improvements increase costs when the benefit is greater.

D.text: It removes every risk
D.rationale: Absurd - no improvement removes every risk.

100.scenario: A technical team wants the service desk to systematically forward every ticket without any initial diagnosis.
100.question_text: Which answer best matches best practice?
100.explanation: The Service Desk is a Single Point of Contact AND performs first-level handling (triage, simple resolution, escalation when needed). It is neither a mere pass-through nor a universal solver.

A.text: The service desk must provide a point of contact and perform first-level handling when appropriate
A.rationale: Exact wording - SPOC + appropriate first handling.

B.text: The service desk must never analyse an incident
B.rationale: False - the SD analyses and categorises; it is not a mere relay.

C.text: The service desk must only create tickets
C.rationale: False - the SD can resolve simple first-level incidents.

D.text: The service desk must always resolve every incident alone
D.rationale: False - the SD escalates to specialist teams when needed.

101.scenario: An interruption is planned to carry out an approved maintenance.
101.question_text: How does this interruption generally influence the availability measure?
101.explanation: The impact of planned maintenance on the availability measure depends on rules defined in the service agreement: some maintenances are excluded from the calculation (Agreed Service Time), others are not. No universal rule.

A.text: According to the measurement rules defined by the organisation
A.rationale: Exact wording - depends on the agreed rules.

B.text: It is always ignored
B.rationale: False - no universal automatic exclusion.

C.text: It is always counted as a major incident
C.rationale: False - planned maintenance is not a major incident.

D.text: It automatically removes SLAs
D.rationale: False - maintenance does not remove SLAs.

102.scenario: A team regularly resolves the same incident but never documents the solution.
102.question_text: Which consequence is the most likely?
102.explanation: Not capitalising on a recurring solution forces re-solving every time - loss of time, quality, dependency on individual expertise. Contrary to ITIL Knowledge Management.

A.text: A loss of efficiency during future handling
A.rationale: Exact wording - systematic loss of efficiency.

B.text: An automatic improvement of resolution times
B.rationale: Absurd - without memory, times do not mechanically improve.

C.text: A reduction in the number of users
C.rationale: No logical link.

D.text: Better governance
D.rationale: No link - governance does not improve because of missing technical documentation.

103.scenario: An outage simultaneously affects several essential services of the company.
103.question_text: Which objective must guide the immediate decisions?
103.explanation: Facing a multi-service major incident, priority is fast restoration + coordination of stakeholders (communication, orchestration, decisions). Root-cause analysis is deferred to Problem Management after the crisis.

A.text: Restore the service as quickly as possible while coordinating stakeholders
A.rationale: Exact wording - restoration + coordination = immediate priority.

B.text: Immediately identify every root cause
B.rationale: False - root-cause analysis comes later, in Problem Management.

C.text: Wait for the next governance meeting
C.rationale: Absurd - waiting for a scheduled meeting during a crisis = negligence.

D.text: Create a new service catalogue
D.rationale: Off-topic - creating a catalogue has nothing to do with crisis management.

104.question_text: Why is stakeholder experience important when evaluating a service?
104.explanation: ITIL places user / customer experience at the heart of perceived value. A technically excellent service with a poor experience will be perceived as low-value - hence the importance of XLA indicators (Experience Level Agreements).

A.text: Because it influences the perception of value
A.rationale: Exact wording - experience directly tied to value perception.

B.text: Because it replaces SLAs
B.rationale: False - experience complements SLAs; it does not replace them.

C.text: Because it automatically determines the budget
C.rationale: False - no direct link between experience and budget.

D.text: Because it removes risks
D.rationale: Absurd - experience does not remove any risk by itself.

105.scenario: An improvement delivers significant benefits but also raises operating costs.
105.explanation: An improvement is judged on the balance between costs, risks, and value (the 3 components of ITIL value). Refusing any cost increase without looking at benefits = an anti-improvement bias.

A.text: Evaluate the overall balance between costs, risks, and value
A.rationale: Exact wording - cost/risk/value balance = ITIL judgement.

B.text: Refuse any cost increase
B.rationale: False - mechanically refusing any increase ignores the benefits.

C.text: Ignore the benefits obtained
C.rationale: Absurd - benefits are precisely the positive side of the trade-off.

D.text: Measure only satisfaction
D.rationale: Reductive - satisfaction is a signal, not the sole criterion.

106.scenario: Two customers use the same service but pursue different business objectives.
106.question_text: Which conclusion is the most relevant?
106.explanation: The same technical service can create different value depending on the consumers' business objectives - value is perceived and contextual. A founding ITIL principle.

A.text: The same service can create different value depending on context
A.rationale: Exact wording - contextual value depending on objectives.

B.text: Both customers will receive exactly the same value
B.rationale: False - perceived value differs by context.

C.text: The provider alone decides the value created
C.rationale: False - value is co-created, not decided by the provider.

D.text: Value depends only on the contract
D.rationale: Reductive - the contract frames things, but value emerges from actual use.

107.question_text: Why must ITIL practices be adapted to the context of each organisation?
107.explanation: ITIL is explicitly a framework of recommendations, not universal procedures. Each organisation adapts practices to its context, size, culture, and regulatory constraints.

A.text: Because ITIL provides recommendations and not universal procedures
A.rationale: Exact wording - ITIL = recommendations to adapt.

B.text: Because each practice has a single official implementation
B.rationale: False - each practice has several possible implementations depending on context.

C.text: Because the practices replace business objectives
C.rationale: Absurd - practices serve business objectives; they do not replace them.

D.text: Because suppliers impose their use
D.rationale: False - suppliers do not dictate ITIL adoption.

108.scenario: A team improves a service without consulting the affected users.
108.question_text: Which risk is the most likely?
108.explanation: Improving a service without consulting the affected users = risk of missing the target. The "collaborate and promote visibility" principle requires involving relevant stakeholders from the start.

A.text: The improvement might not address the real needs
A.rationale: Exact wording - without listening to users, you improve the wrong thing.

B.text: The service will automatically become unavailable
B.rationale: Absurd - no mechanical link between consultation and availability.

C.text: Supplier contracts will be terminated
C.rationale: No link - supplier contracts do not depend on a forgotten user consultation.

D.text: Incidents will completely disappear
D.rationale: Absurd - incidents do not disappear because of a lack of consultation.

109.question_text: Which element should mainly guide decisions about service management?
109.explanation: ITIL: every service management decision must be guided by value creation for stakeholders. It is the compass of the framework, embodied in the "focus on value" principle.

A.text: Value creation for stakeholders
A.rationale: Exact wording - value creation = ITIL compass.

B.text: The number of teams involved
B.rationale: Number of teams = practical consideration, not a decision criterion.

C.text: The complexity of the tools
C.rationale: Tool complexity = symptom to minimise, not a guide.

D.text: The number of existing procedures
D.rationale: Number of procedures = activity measure, not a strategic compass.

110.scenario: After several successful improvements, a team stops measuring the service's performance.
110.question_text: What is the main potential consequence?
110.explanation: Stopping measurement = losing the ability to detect new improvement opportunities and to validate that past gains hold over time. Contrary to continual improvement, which is a perpetual cycle.

A.text: It will become harder to identify new improvement opportunities
A.rationale: Exact wording - without measurement, no more opportunity detection.

B.text: Every service will automatically meet its objectives
B.rationale: Absurd - no automatic objective compliance without measurement.

C.text: Changes will no longer be needed
C.rationale: False - changes remain permanently necessary.

D.text: Incidents will automatically be eliminated
D.rationale: Absurd - incidents do not disappear because of missing measurement.

111.question_text: Which statement best distinguishes a digital product from a digital service according to ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
111.explanation: A digital product is a configuration of resources created to offer value to a consumer. A digital service organises the use of digital products and other resources to facilitate the desired outcomes.

A.text: A digital product is the configuration of resources; a digital service is the organised use of those resources to facilitate outcomes
A.rationale: This distinction matches the ITIL definitions of a digital product and a digital service.

B.text: A digital product is always sold, while a digital service is always provided free of charge
B.rationale: Billing arrangements do not determine whether an offering is a product or a service.

C.text: A digital product belongs to the consumer, while a digital service belongs to the provider
C.rationale: Ownership can vary and is not the distinguishing criterion between the two concepts.

D.text: A digital product is only software, while a digital service only includes people
D.rationale: A product can combine several resources, and a service can mobilise people, technologies, and processes.

112.scenario: A company provides a laptop to a new employee, and ownership of the equipment is transferred to the consumer organisation.
112.question_text: Which component of a service offering is mainly illustrated?
112.explanation: Goods transfer concerns the delivery of an item whose ownership or responsibility passes to the consumer. The laptop here becomes an asset owned by the consumer organisation.

A.text: Goods transfer
A.rationale: Ownership of the equipment is transferred to the consumer.

B.text: Access to resources
B.rationale: Access lets you use a resource without necessarily acquiring ownership.

C.text: A service action
C.rationale: A service action would be an activity performed for the consumer, such as installation or maintenance.

D.text: A service level
D.rationale: A service level is a set of metrics for expected or achieved quality.

113.scenario: A provider backs up a customer's databases every night and checks the execution logs.
113.question_text: Which element of a service offering does this activity represent?
113.explanation: A service action is an activity performed by the provider to meet the consumer's needs. Backup and verification are carried out for the customer without any transfer of ownership.

A.text: A service action
A.rationale: The provider regularly performs an activity for the consumer's benefit.

B.text: Goods transfer
B.rationale: No goods or ownership rights are transferred to the customer.

C.text: Access to resources
C.rationale: The scenario describes an activity performed by the provider, not just a right of use.

D.text: A product prototype
D.rationale: A prototype is used to explore or validate a solution before full implementation.

114.scenario: A customer receives the right to use a hosted analytics platform for twelve months, without becoming the owner of the infrastructure or the software.
114.question_text: Which component of the service offering is described?
114.explanation: Access to resources lets the consumer use resources controlled by the provider without owning them. The temporary right to use the platform matches this component exactly.

A.text: Access to resources
A.rationale: The consumer uses the platform without acquiring the underlying assets.

B.text: Goods transfer
B.rationale: Ownership of the software and infrastructure stays with the provider.

C.text: A service action
C.rationale: The main element here is the right of access, not an activity performed for the customer.

D.text: A collaborative relationship
D.rationale: A collaborative relationship describes a level of partnership, not a component of a service offering.

115.question_text: Which statement best describes a service offering?
115.explanation: A service offering is a formal description of one or more services designed to meet the needs of a target group. It may include service actions, access to resources, and goods transfer.

A.text: A possible combination of service actions, access to resources, and goods transfers aimed at a target group
A.rationale: This statement reflects the possible components of an ITIL service offering.

B.text: An internal list of every technology owned by the provider
B.rationale: A technology inventory describes neither the proposition made to the consumer nor its targeted needs.

C.text: A contract that must always specify a fixed price and a penalty
C.rationale: An offering can exist without these specific contractual terms.

D.text: A business outcome fully guaranteed by the provider
D.rationale: Outcomes depend on value co-creation and are not always solely controlled by the provider.

116.scenario: A company creates an application, publishes new versions, and continually improves the associated service offerings, while a separate partner operates the infrastructure.
116.question_text: Which role does the company mainly perform?
116.explanation: The digital product provider is responsible for the creation and continual improvement of digital products and their associated service offerings. This role may be distinct from the one that operates the infrastructure or provides certain service components.

A.text: Digital product provider
A.rationale: The company creates and improves the digital product and its associated offerings.

B.text: Service consumer
B.rationale: The scenario mainly highlights the responsibility for creating the product, not consuming it.

C.text: Sponsor
C.rationale: The sponsor generally authorises the budget for consuming a service.

D.text: Service desk
D.rationale: The service desk is a point of contact, not a role responsible for product creation.

117.scenario: A telecom operator offers the same standard subscription to thousands of customers, with little personalisation and an identical contract for all.
117.question_text: Which type of service relationship is most likely?
117.explanation: A basic relationship is generally standardised, efficiency-oriented, and characterised by limited personalisation. It suits broadly uniform offerings aimed at many consumers.

A.text: Basic relationship
A.rationale: The standard offering and the low degree of adaptation characterise a basic relationship.

B.text: Cooperative relationship
B.rationale: A cooperative relationship involves more adaptation and joint improvement.

C.text: Collaborative relationship
C.rationale: A collaborative relationship rests on a strategic partnership and strong interdependence.

D.text: Governance relationship
D.rationale: This term is not one of the service relationship types defined in this model.

118.scenario: A managed service provider adapts its processes to a customer's specific requirements, and both parties regularly review operational improvements.
118.question_text: Which type of service relationship is described?
118.explanation: A cooperative relationship includes greater personalisation and regular collaboration aimed at improving services. It goes beyond a standard offering without necessarily reaching the strategic interdependence of a collaborative partnership.

A.text: Cooperative relationship
A.rationale: Process adaptation and joint improvement reviews correspond to active cooperation.

B.text: Basic relationship
B.rationale: A basic relationship is more standardised and focused on transactional efficiency.

C.text: Collaborative relationship
C.rationale: The scenario does not mention shared strategy, shared risks, or strong interdependence.

D.text: Prototype-supplier relationship
D.rationale: This category is not one of the ITIL service relationship types.

119.scenario: Two organisations jointly design a new platform, share risks, coordinate their roadmaps, and strongly depend on each other to reach a common goal.
119.question_text: Which type of service relationship is most appropriate?
119.explanation: A collaborative relationship is strategic and rests on trust, joint innovation, shared risks, and strong interdependence. The organisations pursue growth or common outcomes together.

A.text: Collaborative relationship
A.rationale: Shared strategy, innovation, and interdependence characterise this type of relationship.

B.text: Cooperative relationship
B.rationale: Cooperation may include joint improvements but not necessarily such a strong strategic dependency.

C.text: Basic relationship
C.rationale: A basic relationship favours a standard offering and limited interactions.

D.text: Support relationship
D.rationale: This is not an official service relationship type in this classification.

120.question_text: Which statement about the service journey is correct?
120.explanation: The service journey represents the whole set of activities and interactions performed by the provider and the consumer. It is not necessarily linear and may include loops, parallel steps, and different paths.

A.text: It may include loops, parallel steps, and several possible paths
A.rationale: A service journey reflects real interactions that do not always follow a single sequence.

B.text: It only starts after an SLA is signed
B.rationale: The journey can start from the very first interactions, well before a formal agreement.

C.text: It is carried out only by the service provider
C.rationale: The provider and the consumer both participate in the journey and in value co-creation.

D.text: It ends as soon as the service is made available
D.rationale: The journey also covers use, support, improvement, and possibly the end of the service.

121.question_text: Which of the following best defines service quality?
121.explanation: Service quality is the sum of the characteristics of a service that are relevant to satisfying expressed or implied needs. It cannot be reduced to a single technical metric.

A.text: The sum of the characteristics relevant to satisfying expressed and implied needs
A.rationale: This wording matches the overall definition of service quality.

B.text: The availability percentage measured over a period
B.rationale: Availability may contribute to quality, but it represents only one aspect.

C.text: Satisfaction declared only by the sponsor
C.rationale: Multiple stakeholders' perceptions can count, and quality does not depend on a single role.

D.text: The number of service actions executed by the provider
D.rationale: Activity volume does not demonstrate that the consumer's needs are met.

122.question_text: What is a service level according to ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
122.explanation: A service level is a set of metrics that defines the expected or actually achieved quality. It makes expectations and results precise enough to be tracked and evaluated.

A.text: A set of metrics defining expected or achieved service quality
A.rationale: A service level translates quality into defined metrics.

B.text: A general statement of the provider's vision
B.rationale: A vision gives direction but does not define measurable quality expectations.

C.text: A list of incidents resolved during the month
C.rationale: That list can feed reports but does not by itself constitute a service level.

D.text: A classification of the relationship as basic, cooperative, or collaborative
D.rationale: Relationship types describe the nature of collaboration, not measured quality.

123.question_text: Which statement correctly describes a service level agreement (SLA)?
123.explanation: An SLA is a documented agreement between a service provider and a customer. It identifies the required services and the expected service levels, generally through relevant metrics.

A.text: A documented agreement between provider and customer specifying the services and expected service levels
A.rationale: This proposition covers the essential parties and content of an SLA.

B.text: An internal document defining only the responsibilities of the technical team
B.rationale: An SLA commits the provider and the customer, and is not limited to the internal organisation.

C.text: A report that only presents the levels actually achieved
C.rationale: A report measures results, while an SLA formalises the agreed services and expectations.

D.text: A contract reserved for collaborative relationships
D.rationale: An SLA can be used in different types of service relationships.

124.scenario: A tender requires low-carbon energy, transparent supply chains, and responsible employment practices.
124.question_text: Which service quality concept is mainly involved?
124.explanation: Sustainability ensures that a product or service meets and will continue to meet expectations related to environmental protection, social progress, and economic growth. The requirements described therefore go beyond mere technical performance.

A.text: Sustainability
A.rationale: Environmental, social, and economic criteria directly fall under sustainability.

B.text: Warranty
B.rationale: Warranty concerns assurance that a service will meet agreed conditions of use.

C.text: Utility
C.rationale: Utility describes what the service does and its ability to meet a functional need.

D.text: Observability
D.rationale: Observability concerns inferring the internal state of a system from its outputs.

125.scenario: A company uses an external cloud service to host its own platform, then provides that platform as a service to its customers.
125.question_text: Which statement is the most correct?
125.explanation: The same organisation can take on different roles in several service relationships. It is a consumer with respect to the cloud provider and a provider with respect to the users of its platform.

A.text: The company is a consumer of the cloud and a provider of its platform in two distinct relationships
A.rationale: Roles are determined separately in each service relationship.

B.text: The company can only be a provider because it bills its customers
B.rationale: Providing a service does not prevent simultaneously consuming another service.

C.text: The company can only be a consumer because it depends on external infrastructure
C.rationale: Its dependency on the cloud does not remove its role as provider to its own customers.

D.text: The company is necessarily the sponsor in both relationships
D.rationale: The sponsor authorises the budget and is not automatically the whole organisation in each relationship.

126.question_text: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between PESTLE factors and the four ITIL dimensions?
126.explanation: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental factors are external influences. They can affect each of the four dimensions but do not constitute an additional dimension.

A.text: They influence the four dimensions without forming a fifth dimension
A.rationale: PESTLE helps examine the external environment that acts on all the dimensions.

B.text: They replace the partners and suppliers dimension
B.rationale: Partners and suppliers remain a distinct dimension to consider.

C.text: They only concern information and technology
C.rationale: An external change can also affect people, suppliers, and value streams.

D.text: They are used only when managing major incidents
D.rationale: PESTLE applies to general context analysis, not to a single operational practice.

127.scenario: An organisation finds that its punitive culture prevents teams from reporting mistakes and sharing feedback.
127.question_text: How should this factor be classified?
127.explanation: Organisational culture is an internal factor mainly belonging to organisations and people. It can strongly influence behaviours, collaboration, and improvement.

A.text: An internal factor
A.rationale: Culture is created and maintained within the organisation.

B.text: An external political factor
B.rationale: No government decision or external political dynamic is described.

C.text: An external environmental factor
C.rationale: The scenario is not about the natural environment or ecological sustainability.

D.text: An external technological factor
D.rationale: The issue concerns behaviours and culture, not a technological development.

128.scenario: Strong inflation suddenly raises the costs of licences, energy, and subcontracting contracts.
128.question_text: Which PESTLE factor is mainly illustrated?
128.explanation: Inflation, interest rates, costs, and market conditions are economic factors. They can change sourcing decisions, budgets, and the viability of offerings.

A.text: Economic
A.rationale: Inflation is an economic development directly affecting costs.

B.text: Social
B.rationale: Social factors mainly concern behaviours, expectations, and demographic changes.

C.text: Legal
C.rationale: No new legal obligation is at the origin of the described increase.

D.text: Technological
D.rationale: The technologies concerned cost more, but the triggering factor is economic.

129.scenario: A new regulation requires reducing the carbon footprint of data centres and publishing emission indicators.
129.question_text: Which PESTLE factor is the most directly concerned by the emissions reduction objective?
129.explanation: Reducing the carbon footprint and emissions mainly falls under the environmental factor. The regulation also has a legal dimension, but the question targets the ecological purpose of the requirement.

A.text: Environmental
A.rationale: The main objective concerns the impact on the natural environment.

B.text: Legal
B.rationale: The form of the requirement is regulatory, but its direct object is emissions reduction.

C.text: Social
C.rationale: The scenario does not mainly target social behaviours or demographic trends.

D.text: Economic
D.rationale: Costs may result from it, but they are not the objective described.

130.question_text: Which scope belongs to the "information and technology" dimension?
130.explanation: This dimension covers the information, knowledge, and technologies used both in products and services and in the organisation's management system. It is therefore not limited to user-visible tools or to internal data only.

A.text: The information, knowledge, and technologies used in products, services, and their management
A.rationale: This answer reflects the full scope of the dimension in the four-dimensions model.

B.text: Only technologies directly visible to consumers
B.rationale: The dimension also includes tools, data, and knowledge used to manage products and services.

C.text: Only data that the organisation legally owns
C.rationale: Scope depends on the use of information, not solely on its legal ownership.

D.text: Only technologies operated by external partners
D.rationale: Internal as well as external technologies can fall under this dimension.

131.topic: Introduction to the ITIL product and service lifecycle
131.question_text: Which statement best describes the eight ITIL product and service lifecycle activities?
131.explanation: The activities discover, design, acquire, build, transition, operate, deliver, and support are interconnected. They can be repeated, overlap, and be used in different orders depending on the context.

A.text: They are used iteratively and not necessarily sequentially
A.rationale: The ITIL lifecycle is flexible and allows for loops and parallel activities.

B.text: They must always be completed once in the order given
B.rationale: This linear interpretation does not reflect the iterative nature of the lifecycle.

C.text: Only build and transition can be repeated
C.rationale: Every activity can be revisited when new information appears.

D.text: Each activity must be performed by a different organisation
D.rationale: The distribution of responsibilities depends on the operating model and context.

132.scenario: A team compares suppliers, negotiates terms, and allocates cloud resources to enable the extension of a service.
132.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly being performed?
132.explanation: The "acquire" activity aims to obtain, secure, and effectively allocate the necessary resources. It also takes into account their availability, sustainability, and ability to scale.

A.text: Acquire
A.rationale: Selecting suppliers and allocating resources are directly part of acquisition.

B.text: Build
B.rationale: Building mainly consists of developing, integrating, and testing the solution's components.

C.text: Transition
C.rationale: Transition prepares and moves changes into the environments where they will be used.

D.text: Operate
D.rationale: Operate concerns the ongoing running and monitoring of products and systems.

133.scenario: Developers integrate components, configure the infrastructure, run tests, and produce the solution's documentation.
133.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
133.explanation: Build turns designs into functional solutions by developing, configuring, integrating, and testing components. The necessary documentation can also be produced during this activity.

A.text: Build
A.rationale: The described tasks turn the design into a usable and tested solution.

B.text: Acquire
B.rationale: Acquire obtains the resources but does not mainly cover their technical integration.

C.text: Deliver
C.rationale: Deliver focuses on providing services to users and their routine interactions.

D.text: Discover
D.rationale: Discover aims to understand needs, opportunities, and constraints before implementation.

134.scenario: A team activates accounts for new users, handles routine SLA-covered requests, and collects feedback after use.
134.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly involved?
134.explanation: Deliver aims to provide services to users, notably through onboarding and offboarding users, handling normal interactions, and collecting feedback. It differs from support, which is mainly reactive to incidents.

A.text: Deliver
A.rationale: User onboarding and routine service provision sit at the heart of this activity.

B.text: Operate
B.rationale: Operate maintains and monitors the underlying products and systems.

C.text: Support
C.rationale: Support mainly handles interruptions, difficulties, and assistance needs.

D.text: Design
D.rationale: Design defines the solution and expected experience before delivery.

135.scenario: After a major outage, several teams restore the service, execute disaster recovery, and write a post-incident report.
135.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
135.explanation: Support aims to identify and resolve incidents, restore services, and execute the necessary recovery activities. It also collects information that enables learning after interruptions.

A.text: Support
A.rationale: Restoration, disaster recovery, and post-incident analysis fall under support.

B.text: Deliver
B.rationale: Deliver mainly concerns routine provision of the service, not the response to a major outage.

C.text: Transition
C.rationale: Transition manages the movement of products or changes into their usage environment.

D.text: Acquire
D.rationale: No selection or allocation of new resources is central to the scenario.

136.scenario: Two digital products follow different combinations of value chain activities: one favours frequent releases, the other requires long regulatory validations.
136.question_text: Why can both combinations be ITIL-compliant?
136.explanation: Value chain activities can be combined according to different models to fit the context, the product and service architecture, the objective, and the operating model. ITIL does not prescribe a single sequence.

A.text: Because activities can be combined into patterns tailored to the context and operating model
A.rationale: The value chain allows different combinations depending on how the organisation creates value.

B.text: Because each product can permanently drop the activities that slow its delivery
B.rationale: Adapting a model does not mean ignoring the activities needed for value, control, or quality.

C.text: Because the value chain applies only to unregulated products
C.rationale: It applies to any product and service management context, including regulated ones.

D.text: Because each management practice imposes its own independent value chain
D.rationale: Practices contribute to activities and value streams; they do not each create a separate chain.

137.scenario: A dashboard indicates that a process is working correctly, but observing daily work reveals manual workarounds and unrecorded delays.
137.question_text: Which action best applies the "start where you are" principle?
137.explanation: This principle recommends assessing the current state objectively. Measures are useful, but they must be complemented by direct observation to avoid an incomplete or misleading picture of what exists.

A.text: Combine dashboard data with direct observation of the work
A.rationale: This approach assesses what exists based on both quantitative evidence and what actually happens.

B.text: Trust only the dashboard because measures are objective
B.rationale: A measure can omit workarounds or effects that are not recorded.

C.text: Ignore what exists and immediately redesign the process
C.rationale: The clean-slate approach specifically contradicts the assessment of the current state recommended by this principle.

D.text: Automate the manual steps before understanding their cause
D.rationale: Automating without evaluation risks reinforcing an inefficient way of working.

138.question_text: Why does ITIL describe governance as enabling in nature?
138.explanation: Governance sets direction, exercises oversight, and defines the boundaries within which the organisation can act. It must let teams make responsible decisions rather than centralise every operational action.

A.text: It sets direction and control while enabling teams to manage and act within a clear framework
A.rationale: Enabling governance combines appropriate control with framed autonomy.

B.text: It directly performs every lifecycle activity
B.rationale: Governance directs and oversees, but does not necessarily perform each operational activity.

C.text: It removes the need to delegate decisions
C.rationale: Effective governance can specifically define which decisions are delegated and within what limits.

D.text: It guarantees that no risk will be accepted
D.rationale: Governance frames risk decisions; it does not impose their total elimination.

139.scenario: A team has a detailed description of the requirements for a future service and an interactive mock-up used to gather feedback.
139.question_text: Which terms best correspond to these two items?
139.explanation: A product specification describes the expected requirements, characteristics, and constraints. A prototype is a preliminary representation used to explore, test, or validate ideas before full implementation.

A.text: Product specification and product prototype
A.rationale: The formal description corresponds to the specification and the exploratory mock-up to the prototype.

B.text: SLA and release
B.rationale: An SLA describes services and expected levels, while a release is made available for use.

C.text: Operating model and event
C.rationale: An operating model describes how capabilities are organised, and an event is a significant state change.

D.text: Outcome and output
D.rationale: These terms distinguish a desired effect from a produced deliverable, not the two design artefacts described.

140.scenario: A monitoring tool reports that CPU usage exceeds a threshold, but users have not yet noticed any interruption.
140.question_text: How should this item be classified as a priority?
140.explanation: An event is a significant state change for the management of a service or configuration item. It becomes an incident only if it causes or represents an unplanned interruption or a reduction in quality requiring restoration.

A.text: An event
A.rationale: The exceeded threshold is a significant state change with no observed interruption.

B.text: An incident
B.rationale: No service interruption or degradation is observed yet.

C.text: A known error
C.rationale: No analysed cause or documented workaround is mentioned.

D.text: A service request
D.rationale: The signal is generated by monitoring and is not a predefined user request.

141.question_text: Which statement best describes a release?
141.explanation: A release is a set of new or changed configuration items made available for use. It does not necessarily correspond to every individual modification, nor to an automatic deployment.

A.text: A set of new or changed configuration items made available for use
A.rationale: This phrasing matches the ITIL definition of a release.

B.text: Any code change recorded in the repository
B.rationale: A recorded change may never be grouped or made available in a release.

C.text: The automatic transfer of every change into production
C.rationale: This phrasing rather describes continuous deployment.

D.text: An agreement on a service's quality levels
D.rationale: That notion belongs to SLAs and not to release management.

142.question_text: What is the main role of a test in the product and service lifecycle?
142.explanation: A test evaluates a product, service, or component against predefined criteria. It produces information used to assess its quality, compliance, or fitness for use.

A.text: Evaluate an item against defined criteria to produce information about its quality or compliance
A.rationale: A test provides evidence to support a decision, without guaranteeing the total absence of defects.

B.text: Guarantee that no defect will ever be present
B.rationale: Tests reduce uncertainty but generally cannot prove the total absence of defects.

C.text: Replace observation of the service in production
C.rationale: Pre-release tests and production observation provide complementary information.

D.text: Automatically authorise every release to production
D.rationale: A successful test may contribute to a decision, but does not by itself define the authorisation rules.

143.scenario: With every change, developers frequently merge their code into a shared repository and automated tests quickly detect conflicts.
143.explanation: Continuous integration consists of frequently integrating changes into a common code base and verifying them automatically. Its objective is to quickly detect integration defects.

A.text: Continuous integration
A.rationale: Frequent merges and automated checks are the central characteristics of this practice.

B.text: Continuous delivery
B.rationale: Continuous delivery aims to keep changes in a deployable state, beyond mere integration.

C.text: Continuous deployment
C.rationale: Continuous deployment automatically pushes validated changes into production.

D.text: Observability
D.rationale: Observability concerns understanding the internal state of a running system.

144.scenario: An organisation automates the build and the tests so that any validated update can be deployed to production at any time, but a manager decides case by case when to deploy it.
144.explanation: Continuous delivery keeps changes in a state ready for production release. Deployment remains an explicit decision, unlike continuous deployment where every validated change is automatically put into production.

A.text: Continuous delivery
A.rationale: Changes are always deployable, but their release still requires a decision.

B.text: Continuous deployment
B.rationale: In continuous deployment, the move to production is automatic after validation.

C.text: Continuous integration
C.rationale: Continuous integration frequently checks changes without alone guaranteeing they are ready to be delivered.

D.text: Release management
D.rationale: Release management coordinates what is made available but does not specifically denote this automated capability.

145.scenario: Every change that passes the automated tests is pushed to production without additional authorisation.
145.explanation: Continuous deployment automates the move to production of every change that meets the defined controls. It differs from continuous delivery, where a separate decision to deploy remains.

A.text: Continuous deployment
A.rationale: Automatic release to production after validation is the distinguishing criterion.

B.text: Continuous delivery
B.rationale: Continuous delivery ensures a deployable state but may retain a manual authorisation.

C.text: Continuous integration
C.rationale: Continuous integration does not require changes to be automatically pushed to production.

D.text: Manual transition
D.rationale: The scenario specifically states that no additional authorisation or intervention is required.

146.explanation: Reliability is the ability of a product, service, or configuration item to perform its intended function over a specified period or number of cycles. It differs from availability and recoverability.

A.text: The ability to perform the intended function over a specified duration or number of cycles
A.rationale: This answer reflects the notion of correct and lasting operation associated with reliability.

B.text: The ability to explain every internal state from metrics
B.rationale: This phrasing describes observability rather than reliability.

C.text: The ability to restore a service after any interruption
C.rationale: Restoration belongs to resilience, recovery, and support, not to reliability alone.

D.text: The proportion of requests closed within the agreed timeframe
D.rationale: This is a processing metric, not a definition of reliability.

147.scenario: An organisation makes a team responsible for improving service reliability through measurable objectives, automation, and close collaboration with product teams.
147.explanation: Site Reliability Engineering applies software engineering principles to operations to obtain scalable, reliable services. It relies notably on automation, reliability objectives, and shared responsibility.

A.text: Site Reliability Engineering
A.rationale: The combination of engineering, automation, and reliability objectives matches SRE.

B.text: Relationship management
B.rationale: This practice develops relationships with stakeholders and does not define this operational engineering approach.

C.text: Service request management
C.rationale: It handles predefined user requests, not reliability engineering.

D.text: Service design
D.rationale: Design can incorporate reliability but does not denote the operational approach described.

148.explanation: Observability is the ability to determine or infer the internal state of a system from its outputs, such as logs, metrics, and traces. It does not simply correspond to collecting an isolated indicator.

A.text: The ability to infer the internal state of a system from its outputs
A.rationale: This wording precisely expresses the link between observable outputs and internal state.

B.text: The guarantee that a service always meets its SLA
B.rationale: Observability provides information but does not guarantee contractual performance.

C.text: Monitoring a single availability indicator
C.rationale: An isolated measure generally does not explain complex internal states.

D.text: Documenting all contractual dependencies
D.rationale: This activity concerns relationships and suppliers rather than a system's technical state.

149.scenario: A flood makes the primary site unusable and threatens the continuity of several critical services.
149.question_text: Which ITIL term best describes this situation?
149.explanation: A disaster is a sudden, unplanned event that causes significant damage or losses and requires a coordinated response. It generally exceeds the scope of an ordinary operational incident.

A.text: A disaster
A.rationale: The flood produces major effects requiring recovery and continuity capabilities.

B.text: A standard event
B.rationale: An event is a significant state change, but this term does not convey the destructive scale described.

C.text: A service request
C.rationale: A service request is a predefined request initiated by a user or their representative.

D.text: A known error
D.rationale: A known error is an analysed problem whose cause or workaround is documented.

150.scenario: A team has identified that a design defect causes recurring outages. The cause is understood and a workaround is documented, but the defect is not yet fixed.
150.question_text: How should this item be classified?
150.explanation: A known error is a problem that has been analysed but is not yet resolved. Its cause, its workaround, or both are generally documented to help handle the associated incidents.

A.text: A known error
A.rationale: The cause and workaround are known while the permanent fix remains to be done.

B.text: A major incident
B.rationale: An incident is a specific interruption, whereas the item described is the analysed underlying defect.

C.text: An event
C.rationale: An event indicates a state change and does not necessarily represent a known cause.

D.text: A service request
D.rationale: The defect is not a standard predefined user request.

151.question_text: What is an operating model according to ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
151.explanation: An operating model represents the way an organisation configures and coordinates its capabilities and resources to fulfil its objective. It links strategy to the concrete organisation of work.

A.text: A representation of how capabilities and resources are organised to fulfil the organisation's objective
A.rationale: This answer describes the structuring function of the operating model.

B.text: A mock-up intended to test a product's interface
B.rationale: This description matches a product prototype.

C.text: A set of metrics defining a service's quality
C.rationale: This definition matches a service level.

D.text: A list of all approved suppliers
D.rationale: A supplier register is only one possible element of the organisation's resources.

152.question_text: What are the two groups of management practices identified in ITIL Foundation (Version 5)?
152.explanation: Version 5 distinguishes general management practices and product and service management practices. This organisation reflects both the organisation's common capabilities and those directly oriented towards its products and services.

A.text: General management practices and product and service management practices
A.rationale: These two headings match the practice groups presented in the syllabus.

B.text: Strategic practices and tactical practices
B.rationale: ITIL does not split the syllabus practices along this opposition.

C.text: In-house practices and outsourced practices
C.rationale: A single practice can mobilise internal and external resources.

D.text: Mandatory practices and optional practices
D.rationale: ITIL recommends adapting practices to context rather than classifying them this way.

153.question_text: Why does the structure of the ITIL practice guides include chapters such as organisations and people, information and technology, partners and suppliers, and value streams and processes?
153.explanation: The guides examine each practice through the four dimensions to avoid a view limited to processes or tools. This structure favours a balanced implementation adapted to context.

A.text: To address each practice in a balanced way across the four dimensions
A.rationale: The structure explicitly links practices to the four-dimensions model.

B.text: To require four separate teams for each practice
B.rationale: The dimensions are analytical perspectives and do not prescribe an organisational structure.

C.text: To replace the value chain with four processes
C.rationale: The four dimensions complement the value chain without replacing it.

D.text: To classify practices by their maturity level
D.rationale: The titles cited correspond to the dimensions, not to maturity levels.

154.scenario: An organisation wants to improve incident management without inventing its own method from scratch.
154.question_text: What main benefit do the ITIL practice guides bring?
154.explanation: The guides provide consistent, detailed, adaptable recommendations concerning the people, technologies, partners, and value streams of a practice. They speed up adoption of good practice without imposing an identical procedure on every organisation.

A.text: Consistent and adaptable recommendations covering several dimensions of a practice
A.rationale: The guides offer a structured base that must be tailored to the organisation's context.

B.text: A mandatory procedure guaranteeing the same results in every organisation
B.rationale: ITIL is not prescriptive to the point of guaranteeing identical results regardless of context.

C.text: A complete replacement for the teams' experience
C.rationale: The recommendations complement local knowledge and do not make it useless.

D.text: A list of certified software products to buy
D.rationale: The guides describe capabilities and methods, not a mandatory tool catalogue.

155.question_text: Which statement correctly distinguishes a metric from a critical success factor (CSF)?
155.explanation: A critical success factor describes a condition essential to achieving an objective. A metric is a measure or set of data used to evaluate an aspect of performance or progress.

A.text: A CSF expresses an essential success condition; a metric measures an aspect of performance
A.rationale: This distinction separates what must be true to succeed from what is measured.

B.text: A CSF is always numerical; a metric is always qualitative
B.rationale: It is generally the metric that is quantifiable, while the CSF expresses a condition.

C.text: A metric sets the strategy; a CSF records incidents
C.rationale: These functions match the definition of neither term.

D.text: Both terms are synonymous in the practice guides
D.rationale: They are related but play distinct roles in performance management.

156.scenario: Handling a customer order directly produces the paid service, while onboarding a new supplier supports that handling without directly delivering the outcome to the external customer.
156.question_text: How should these two streams be classified?
156.explanation: A core value stream directly delivers value to an external customer. An enabling stream supports one or more core streams by providing the capabilities, resources, or conditions they need.

A.text: The first is core and the second is enabling
A.rationale: The order directly creates customer value, while supplier onboarding supports that creation.

B.text: Both are core because they produce outputs
B.rationale: Producing an output does not mean the stream directly delivers value to an external customer.

C.text: Both are enabling because they use internal resources
C.rationale: Using internal resources does not determine the stream's classification.

D.text: The first is enabling and the second is core
D.rationale: This proposal reverses each stream's direct link to the value delivered to the customer.

157.scenario: A team applies a very detailed procedure to an unprecedented incident involving several suppliers and unpredictable behaviours. The procedure slows the response and hides new information.
157.question_text: Which ITIL approach would be the most appropriate?
157.explanation: Complex thinking recognises that some situations exhibit many interactions, uncertainty, and emergent behaviours. The team should experiment, learn, and adapt its approach rather than assume that a detailed procedure can anticipate everything.

A.text: Use complex thinking and adapt the approach to the level of uncertainty
A.rationale: The unprecedented incident and unpredictable interactions call for an adaptive response.

B.text: Add more mandatory steps to the existing procedure
B.rationale: Additional prescription can make things worse when cause-and-effect relationships are not predictable.

C.text: Remove all coordination between suppliers
C.rationale: Complexity requires more information sharing, not isolation of participants.

D.text: Treat the incident as an enabling value stream without further analysis
D.rationale: Classifying the stream does not resolve the uncertainty or the need to adapt the method.

158.topic: Purpose of value stream mapping and management
158.scenario: An organisation maps its release value stream once, fixes two bottlenecks, and then does not review it again for three years.
158.explanation: Mapping produces a useful representation of the stream's state at a point in time. Value stream management, however, must be ongoing to track changes, measure performance, and identify new improvement opportunities.

A.text: Move from one-off mapping to ongoing value stream management
A.rationale: A value stream evolves with the organisation's products, technologies, teams, and constraints.

B.text: Keep the initial map as the definitive model
B.rationale: An old map may no longer represent how value actually flows.

C.text: Replace the map with a hierarchical org chart
C.rationale: An org chart describes reporting structures, not the path of value creation.

D.text: Only measure the number of steps removed
D.rationale: Reducing step count alone does not demonstrate an improvement in value or performance.

159.scenario: An AI system detects recurring incident trends, forecasts a load increase, and identifies bottlenecks in a value stream.
159.question_text: Which capability from the ITIL AI Capability Model is mainly being used?
159.explanation: Cognition covers analysis, reasoning, pattern detection, and the production of information to support decisions. The system is not merely creating content or communicating: it interprets operational data.

A.text: Cognition
A.rationale: Trend recognition, forecasting, and analysis fall squarely under cognition.

B.text: Creation
B.rationale: Creation is mainly about generating new content or artefacts.

C.text: Communication
C.rationale: Communication is about transmitting and adapting information for its audience.

D.text: Coordination
D.rationale: Coordination organises actions and interactions, but is not the central analytical capability in this scenario.

160.scenario: An organisation uses ITIL to continually manage its products and services. It also launches a temporary initiative, with a business case, project governance, and defined deliverables, to replace a platform.
160.question_text: How does PRINCE2 best complement ITIL in this situation?
160.explanation: PRINCE2 provides a structured method to direct and manage a temporary project, while ITIL frames the continual management and improvement of products and services. The two approaches are complementary rather than competing.

A.text: PRINCE2 structures the temporary project, while ITIL frames the continual management of products and services
A.rationale: Each framework addresses a distinct need and both can be integrated in the same organisation.

B.text: PRINCE2 replaces every ITIL practice for the duration of the project
B.rationale: Service management practices remain useful during the project and for existing services.

C.text: ITIL must be paused until the PRINCE2 project closes
C.rationale: The continual management of products and services does not stop when a project is launched.

D.text: PRINCE2 only applies to projects without a digital component
D.rationale: PRINCE2 can be applied to many types of projects, including digital ones.

161.question_text: Which role authorises the budget dedicated to consuming a service?
161.explanation: The sponsor authorises the funding for consuming the service within the consumer organisation.

A.text: The sponsor
A.rationale: This role authorises the budget needed to consume the service.

B.text: The user
B.rationale: The user directly uses the service but does not necessarily authorise its funding.

C.text: The customer
C.rationale: The customer defines requirements and is accountable for the consumption outcomes, without being necessarily the budget authority.

D.text: The change authority
D.rationale: It authorises changes and not the budget for consuming a service.

162.question_text: How does a service provider mainly contribute to value creation for the consumer?
162.explanation: The provider brings specialised resources and helps reduce certain risks, while value remains co-created with the consumer.

A.text: By providing specialised resources and reducing certain risks
A.rationale: The provider's specialisation complements the consumer's resources and capabilities.

B.text: By taking over all the consumer's responsibilities
B.rationale: Responsibilities remain shared in the service relationship.

C.text: By directly guaranteeing the consumer's financial results
C.rationale: Outcomes depend on many factors that the provider does not control alone.

D.text: By removing every resource need at the consumer
D.rationale: The consumer must still contribute to value co-creation.

163.question_text: In which part of a practice guide are recommendations for the practice's successful automation mainly found?
163.explanation: Recommendations about tools, data, and automations mainly belong to the "information and technology" dimension.

A.text: Information and technology
A.rationale: This dimension addresses technologies and their use to support the practice.

B.text: Organizations and people
B.rationale: This part deals mainly with roles, skills, structures, and human aspects.

C.text: Partners and suppliers
C.rationale: This part examines external relationships and dependencies.

D.text: Value streams and processes
D.rationale: This part mostly describes the activities, controls, and flow of work.

164.scenario: A team runs scheduled backups, monitors systems, and captures technical events.
164.question_text: Which lifecycle activity is mainly illustrated?
164.explanation: The "operate" activity maintains the ongoing running of products, services, and systems, notably through monitoring and recurring tasks.

A.text: Operate
A.rationale: Backups and monitoring are routine operational activities.

B.text: Support
B.rationale: Support focuses mainly on interruptions and assistance needs.

C.text: Deliver
C.rationale: Deliver concerns normal interactions with users and provision of the service.

D.text: Transition
D.rationale: Transition moves changes into the environments where they will be used.

165.question_text: Which criterion is particularly relevant when an organisation evaluates a service provided by a third party in the "acquire" activity?
165.explanation: The organisation must examine the quality, fit, risks, and capacity of external resources or services to support the desired outcomes.

A.text: The quality and fit of the resources or services obtained
A.rationale: Acquisition must ensure that external resources meet needs.

B.text: The speed of restoring internal incidents only
B.rationale: That measure mainly concerns operational support.

C.text: The number of prototypes produced
C.rationale: A prototype belongs more to exploration and design.

D.text: The volume of calls received by the service desk
D.rationale: That data does not directly determine the quality of the acquired resource.

166.question_text: Which statement best describes a good in the context of a service offering?
166.explanation: A good is a tangible or transferable resource whose ownership or responsibility can pass from the provider to the consumer. It differs from temporary access to a resource and from an action performed by the provider.

A.text: A resource transferred to the consumer, who may then take ownership or responsibility for it
A.rationale: Transfer to the consumer is the characteristic that distinguishes a good in a service offering.

B.text: An activity performed by the provider to meet a consumer need
B.rationale: This proposal describes a service action and not a good.

C.text: A right of use granted without transfer of ownership
C.rationale: This proposal matches access to resources.

D.text: A set of agreed metrics for measuring quality
D.rationale: This proposal describes a service level.

167.question_text: Which of the following best describes user experience?
167.explanation: User experience gathers the perceptions and reactions of a person resulting from the actual or anticipated use of a product or service. It can form before, during, and after the interaction.

A.text: A user's perceptions and reactions before, during, and after using a product or service
A.rationale: Experience covers all perceptions related to actual or anticipated use.

B.text: The number of interactions recorded by the service desk
B.rationale: Interaction volume is an operational measure and does not represent the user's perception.

C.text: The product's technical compliance with its specification
C.rationale: Compliance may influence experience, but does not define it.

D.text: The service level accepted only by the sponsor
D.rationale: A service level is a set of agreed metrics, not the experience felt.

168.question_text: Which ITIL term denotes a person or group of persons with functions, responsibilities, authorities, and relationships of their own for achieving objectives?
168.explanation: An organization can be a complete entity or an identifiable part of a larger entity. It is defined by its functions, responsibilities, authorities, and relationships.

A.text: Organization
A.rationale: This definition matches the ITIL term "organization".

B.text: Management practice
B.rationale: A practice is a set of organisational resources designed for performing work.

C.text: Value stream
C.rationale: A value stream is a series of steps used to create and deliver value.

D.text: Service offering
D.rationale: An offering describes the services, goods, and access proposed to a group of consumers.

169.question_text: Which statement about the service consumer role is correct?
169.explanation: The service consumer is a generic role that can include the customer, user, and sponsor roles. A person or group can hold several of these roles depending on the context.

A.text: It can encompass the customer, user, and sponsor roles
A.rationale: These three roles are possible specialisations of the service consumer.

B.text: It refers only to the person who directly uses the service
B.rationale: This definition matches the user role more precisely.

C.text: It refers only to the person who authorises the budget
C.rationale: That responsibility belongs to the sponsor.

D.text: It necessarily refers to an organisation external to the provider
D.rationale: The consumer can be internal or external depending on the service relationship.

170.question_text: Which elements together make up a service relationship?
170.explanation: A service relationship includes service provision, service consumption, and the ongoing management of the relationship between the parties. These elements support value co-creation.

A.text: Service provision, service consumption, and service relationship management
A.rationale: These three elements form the service relationship in ITIL.

B.text: Utility, warranty, and service level agreement only
B.rationale: These elements describe aspects of the service but not all the components of the relationship.

C.text: Incident, problem, and change
C.rationale: These are operational management concepts, not components of a service relationship.

D.text: Discover, build, and operate only
D.rationale: These activities belong to the product and service lifecycle.

171.scenario: A provider manages its resources, gives access to a platform, performs agreed backups, and reports on service levels.
171.question_text: Which set of activities is mainly described?
171.explanation: Service provision includes managing the provider's resources, granting access, performing the agreed actions, and managing service levels. It represents the provider's contribution to the relationship.

A.text: Service provision
A.rationale: All the activities cited are performed by the provider within the service relationship.

B.text: Service consumption
B.rationale: Consumption mainly describes the activities and resources mobilised on the consumer's side.

C.text: Incident management
C.rationale: No unplanned interruption requiring restoration is described.

D.text: Value stream mapping
D.rationale: The scenario describes execution of the service, not its representation as a flow.

172.scenario: A company assigns employees to use a platform, receives the agreed actions from the provider, and uses the resources it has access to.
172.question_text: Which set of activities is mainly described?
172.explanation: Service consumption covers managing the consumer's resources, using the accessible resources, and receiving the agreed actions or goods. It complements service provision.

A.text: Service consumption
A.rationale: The activities described are performed on the consumer's side to use the service.

B.text: Service provision
B.rationale: Provision concerns the activities and resources managed by the provider.

C.text: Service design
C.rationale: The scenario concerns ongoing use rather than defining a future solution.

D.text: Governance
D.rationale: Governance evaluates, directs, and monitors rather than directly using the service.

173.scenario: An outsourced payroll service removes the operating cost of an old server but adds subscription and migration fees.
173.question_text: Which cost analysis best fits ITIL?
173.explanation: A service can remove some costs from the consumer while imposing others. Evaluating value must consider both categories rather than only the sticker price.

A.text: Compare the costs the service removes with the costs it imposes on the consumer
A.rationale: ITIL distinguishes costs removed and costs introduced by service consumption.

B.text: Consider only the monthly subscription amount
B.rationale: That approach ignores the removed costs as well as other consumption costs.

C.text: Consider that any cost transferred to the provider disappears for the consumer
C.rationale: The consumer may still bear those costs indirectly through the price or through other resources.

D.text: Evaluate only the provider's internal costs
D.rationale: The consumer's value perception depends on its own costs and outcomes.

174.scenario: A cloud solution reduces the risk of a local hardware failure but introduces dependency on the internet connection and on the provider.
174.question_text: Which conclusion is the most appropriate?
174.explanation: Consuming a service can reduce some risks and introduce new ones. The decision must evaluate the whole risk profile rather than assume a service eliminates all uncertainty.

A.text: The service removes some risks while potentially imposing others
A.rationale: This answer reflects the two possible effects of a service on the consumer's risks.

B.text: Moving to the cloud eliminates every operational risk
B.rationale: The scenario specifically shows new dependencies appearing.

C.text: The introduced risks become exclusively the provider's responsibility
C.rationale: Responsibilities and risks remain shared based on the relationship and agreements.

D.text: Risk should only be assessed after an incident
D.rationale: Risk must be considered before and during service consumption.

175.question_text: Which elements mainly contribute to determining whether a service is fit for use?
175.explanation: Warranty concerns the assurance that a service will meet agreed conditions of use. It is generally associated with availability, capacity, continuity, and security.

A.text: Availability, capacity, continuity, and security
A.rationale: These conditions are the main aspects used to assess warranty.

B.text: Features, outcomes, outputs, and costs
B.rationale: Features mainly belong to utility, while the other terms are not the four warranty conditions.

C.text: Culture, skills, suppliers, and processes
C.rationale: These elements belong to the four management dimensions.

D.text: Discover, design, build, and deliver
D.rationale: These are lifecycle activities, not warranty conditions.

176.question_text: Which proposition best represents the aspects that together influence a service's quality?
176.explanation: Service quality is broader than a single technical measure. It can be assessed through the service's utility, warranty, experience, and sustainability.

A.text: Utility, warranty, experience, and sustainability
A.rationale: These aspects together contribute to the service's ability to meet needs.

B.text: Only availability and resolution time
B.rationale: These measures can be useful but do not cover all of quality.

C.text: Only the provider's costs and risks
C.rationale: Quality is assessed relative to needs and experience, not just provider factors.

D.text: The number of releases and changes performed
D.rationale: The volume of modifications does not demonstrate the quality achieved.

177.scenario: A provider gradually replaces its technicians' manual interventions with self-service and controlled automations.
177.question_text: Why can this shift be advantageous for a digital service?
177.explanation: Reducing manual actions can improve scalability, speed, and consistency, provided the necessary controls and assistance remain in place. The goal is not to eliminate every useful interaction.

A.text: It lets the provider serve more consumers with faster, more consistent execution
A.rationale: Automation and self-service reduce dependency on repetitive manual interventions.

B.text: It guarantees that human support will never again be needed
B.rationale: Some complex or sensitive situations continue to require human intervention.

C.text: It automatically turns every access to a resource into a goods transfer
C.rationale: The execution mode does not change the nature of the offering component.

D.text: It removes the provider's responsibility for quality
D.rationale: The provider remains accountable for the agreed commitments and quality.

178.scenario: A software vendor develops an application sold to an integrator. The integrator then uses it to deliver a managed service to its own customers.
178.question_text: Which statement best describes the vendor's role?
178.explanation: The digital product provider creates and improves the product but does not necessarily deliver the final service to users. Several organisations can therefore contribute to a single offering.

A.text: It provides the digital product without necessarily being the provider of the final service
A.rationale: Product development and service delivery can belong to different organisations.

B.text: It is automatically the sponsor of every end customer
B.rationale: The sponsor belongs to the consumer organisation and authorises the budget.

C.text: It necessarily becomes the user of the managed service
C.rationale: Producing the application does not mean it consumes the final service.

D.text: It must own every infrastructure used by the integrator
D.rationale: Infrastructure ownership depends on the sourcing model and is not imposed by this role.

179.scenario: An initially standardised relationship evolves after several years towards a shared roadmap, joint investments, and shared risks.
179.question_text: Which statement is the most correct?
179.explanation: The service relationship type is not necessarily permanent. It can evolve as trust, interdependence, and the parties' strategic objectives change.

A.text: The relationship can evolve from a basic relationship into a collaborative one
A.rationale: Joint investments and shared risks indicate a shift towards strategic collaboration.

B.text: A basic relationship can never change category
B.rationale: Relationships can evolve depending on needs and the partnership's maturity.

C.text: The relationship automatically becomes a service offering
C.rationale: An offering describes what is proposed, whereas the scenario concerns the nature of the relationship.

D.text: The relationship stops being a service relationship as soon as risks are shared
D.rationale: Shared risks are on the contrary characteristic of a more collaborative relationship.

180.question_text: Which statement best distinguishes a service level from overall service quality?
180.explanation: A service level translates certain aspects of quality into defined metrics. Overall quality remains broader and also includes characteristics or perceptions not fully captured by those metrics.
